title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Body as a Temple
summary: Paul rebukes believers for suing one another before pagan courts and asks why they will not rather be wronged. He reminds them that the unrighteous will not inherit God's kingdom, and that some of them had lived that way before they were washed, sanctified, and justified. He then answers slogans that treated the body as unimportant, insisting that the body belongs to the Lord, will be raised, and is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
story: Chapter 5 dealt with sexual sin the church tolerated; this chapter first turns aside to another way the church was failing to act as a community (taking one another to court) and then returns to sexual morality with a deeper argument. The link between the two halves is the question of what it means to belong to God's kingdom and to Christ. Paul keeps pointing forward: the saints will judge the world (verse 2), the wicked will not inherit the kingdom (verse 9), and God will raise our bodies (verse 14). That future-facing logic prepares for chapter 15, where the resurrection of the body becomes the letter's final theme, and for chapter 7, where Paul answers the church's own questions about marriage.
historical:
Corinth was a Roman colony, and its courts worked under Roman civil law. Civil suits were heard by magistrates or appointed judges, and the system favored people of wealth and rank: those of higher status could sue those beneath them, but it was difficult for a lower-status person to win against a social superior, and litigation was often a public contest for honor. Paul's words suggest that some better-off believers were using the courts against fellow Christians over “everyday matters” (verse 4), property and business disputes, rather than serious crimes.

Jewish communities in the Diaspora often settled disputes among themselves rather than before Gentile authorities, and Paul expects the church to be able to do the same. He grounds the expectation in the Jewish hope that God's people will share in judging the world at the end, an idea found in Daniel 7:22, where judgment is given to the saints of the Most High.
cultural:
Paul quotes slogans that were circulating in the church and then answers them. The translation marks them with quotation marks: “Everything is permissible for me” (verse 12) and “Food for the stomach and the stomach for food” (verse 13). The first may have begun as a garbled version of Paul's own teaching about freedom from the law. The second seems to have reasoned that because food and the stomach will pass away, bodily appetites, including sexual ones, don't matter to the spirit. Many Greeks thought of the body as a lesser shell for the soul, and some concluded that what the body did was morally indifferent.

Prostitution was legal and common in Roman cities, and sex with slaves or prostitutes was widely accepted for men, especially after banquets. The ancient geographer Strabo reported that the temple of Aphrodite in old Corinth had more than a thousand temple courtesans, but that description concerns the Greek city destroyed in 146 BC, and many historians doubt it; there is no need to assume cult prostitution to explain Paul's warning. The closing image, “you were bought at a price” (verse 20), would have been heard against the slave market: a purchased slave belonged to a new master.
literary: The chapter falls into three units. Verses 1 to 8 are a rebuke built on rhetorical questions and irony (“Is there really no one among you wise enough...?” to a church proud of its wisdom). Verses 9 to 11 set a vice list, a common form in ancient moral writing, against a dramatic reversal: “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed.” Verses 12 to 20 are a diatribe, the ancient teaching style in which a speaker quotes an opponent's claim and then answers it. The question “Do you not know” (once as “don't you know”) occurs six times in the chapter, pressing the church to act on what it already knows. The argument ends not with a rule but with a command rooted in ownership: “Therefore glorify God with your body.”

outline.t: Who inherits the kingdom, and what you were
Answering the slogans: the body is for the Lord
Members of Christ and the prostitute
Flee immorality: the body as the Spirit's temple

doctrines.note: Verse 11 gathers the whole of salvation into three verbs: washed, sanctified, justified, all “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” The past is real, but it is past; a person's identity is now defined by what God has done.

The Holy Spirit lives in the believer, making the body itself a temple (verse 19). Paul used the same image for the church as a whole in 3:16; here he applies it to each person's body, which is why bodily conduct is a spiritual matter.

Against the view that the body is a disposable shell, Paul teaches that the body is “for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” and will be raised (verses 13 and 14). Sexual union joins whole persons, echoing Genesis 2:24, and so it cannot be spiritually neutral.
The kingdom of God is something believers will inherit, a future reality that already shapes present conduct. The saints' share in judging the world makes petty lawsuits among them an absurdity.

words.note: Hagiazo, to sanctify or make holy, to set apart for God. In verse 11 it stands in the past tense beside washing and justification, describing a decisive act of God that has already made believers his, rather than a gradual process. Paul calls the Corinthians saints (holy ones) for this reason, even while correcting them.

Dikaioo, to justify, to declare or put in the right. It is a courtroom word, fitting in a chapter that began with lawsuits. The believers who were suing each other for their rights have already been acquitted in God's court, not by their own claims but in Christ's name.

Naos, temple, specifically the inner sanctuary where a god was believed to dwell, as opposed to the wider temple precincts. Calling the body a naos of the Holy Spirit means God himself is present there, which gives the body a dignity and a claim that no Greek theory of the soul could give it.

Agorazo, to buy, from agora, the marketplace. “You were bought at a price” (verse 20; repeated in 7:23) uses the language of purchase, including the purchase of slaves. Believers belong to a new owner, and the price, though unnamed here, is Christ's death.

christ: This chapter shows what union with Christ means in the most concrete terms. Believers' bodies are “members of Christ” (verse 15), joined to him so closely that Paul can say “he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit” (verse 17). The same God who raised Jesus will raise them (verse 14), so the resurrection of Christ is the ground of Christian bodily ethics. Justification and sanctification come “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 11), and the price of their purchase points to the cross. And Paul's shocking suggestion that believers should prefer to be wronged rather than sue (verse 7) echoes the teaching and example of Jesus, who did not retaliate.

hard.q: What do the words in verse 9 translated “men who submit to or perform homosexual acts” mean, and how do Christians read them today?
hard.a:
The phrase translates two Greek words. The first, malakoi, literally means soft ones and was used of men regarded as effeminate, often the passive partner in male sexual relations. The second, arsenokoitai, is rare and may be a term formed from the Greek wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which forbid a man lying with a male. The historic and still majority reading in the church, Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant, takes Paul to be prohibiting same-sex sexual acts as such, consistent with Romans 1:26-27 and the creation pattern of Genesis 2. Some modern interpreters argue that the words had a narrower target in Paul's world, such as exploitative relations with boys or slaves, or male prostitution, and so do not address committed relationships; defenders of the traditional reading answer that the Levitical background is general and that Paul's wider teaching grounds sexual ethics in creation. The debate is sharp and continuing.

Whatever view readers take, the passage's own shape matters. The list places these acts beside greed, drunkenness, theft, and verbal abuse, sins common to everyone in the room, and the next verse addresses real people: “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed.” Paul writes not to shame one group but to call the whole church to a holiness that Christ has already made possible.

questions: Paul asks, “Why not rather be wronged?” When have you seen someone give up a right for the sake of peace or witness, and what did it cost them?
The Corinthians thought what they did with their bodies didn't affect their spiritual lives. Where do people still assume that?
Verse 11 describes people whose past no longer defines them. How does that change the way a church should treat someone with a troubled history?
